Lantern Tiles is a browser puzzle game where you light a dark board one hexagon at a time. Each lantern you place lights the six tiles around it, and the goal is to light the whole board before your oil runs out. It is a small game, made by one person, and you can finish the first chapter in about twenty minutes. I played it over a weekend and I want to write down what I thought while it is still fresh.

The first thing you notice is how quiet it is. There is no music at the start, only a low hum and the click of a tile turning over. The board is almost black, and the only colour is the warm light of the lanterns. It looks like a photo of a city at night taken from a plane. I liked that a lot more than I expected to.

The rules are simple but they get deep quickly. A lantern costs one unit of oil, and you start each level with a fixed amount. Some tiles are mirrors that bounce the light two tiles further. Some are fog tiles that only light up if two lanterns touch them. Later levels add wind, which blows out any lantern on the edge of the board after three turns. By the end of chapter two I was planning five moves ahead. It is a game-changing design for a puzzle game of this size!

The best level in the game is the one called The Harbour. The board is shaped like a bay, with water tiles that never light, and you have exactly enough oil if you use every mirror. I tried it eleven times. When it finally worked, the whole harbour lit up in one sweep and the music came in for the first time. It is one of the best moments I have had in a small game this year.

Not everything works. The undo button only goes back one move, so a mistake early in a long level means starting again. The fog tiles are hard to read on a phone, because the grey is very close to the black of an unlit tile. And the last chapter leans on wind so much that it starts to feel like a timing game rather than a puzzle game.

The controls are simple. You click a tile to place a lantern, right-click to remove it, and press the space bar to end the turn. On a phone you tap and hold instead of right-clicking, which works but is slow. There is no keyboard-only way to move between tiles, which matters if you cannot use a mouse.

Compared with other light puzzles I have played, Lantern Tiles is shorter and calmer. It does not have a story, and it does not need one. It has about forty levels, a level editor that is still marked as early, and no account or sign-in. It runs well in a browser on an old laptop.

If you like slow puzzles where the answer arrives all at once, it is worth an evening. I would wait for a fix to the undo button before playing the last chapter. [Click here](/projects/lantern-tiles/) to play it.
